To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the likelihood ratios for the ACMG/AMP criteria “PM1, PM2 and PM3, as applied to the Li‐Fraumeni Syndrome (LFS) gene, TP53, were significantly different in a cohort of patients who were tested by single gene testing (SGT, 1,000 patients) versus those tested by multi‐gene panel (MGPT, 15,000 patients).
the use of phenotype‐related variant classifications criteria can be affected by patient ascertainment.

the likelihood ratio for a TP53‐associated personal history of cancer is higher in MGPT than in SGT, and this difference is almost certainly explained, and therefore expected, by differences in probands' personal and family history of cancer between these two streams of testing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of phenotype‐related criteria to predict the pathogenicity of variants in TP53, and how these criteria are affected by the ascertainment of the proband.
the impact of ascertainment on the use of gene/syndrome‐specific ACMG/AMP criteria, using the example of the TP53‐related Li–Fraumenie Syndrome.
the use of gene and phenotype‐related variant classifications in the clinical setting, and we demonstrate that differences in patient ascertainment can affect their utility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of gene/syndrome‐specified ACMG‐criteria is a reasonable way to improve the utility of these guidelines, but that the weight of patient phenotype should be determined by the ascertainment of the proband population.
a personal history of TP53‐associated cancer in a proband is a strong indicator of pathogenicity in a variant, with greater weight in a multi‐gene testing setting than a single‐gene testing setting.

, for TP53‐associated cancer, the personal history of TP53‐associated malignancies is more predictive of pathogenesis in the MGPT cohort, which may be explained by differences in patient ascertainment between SGT and MGPT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of gene/condition‐specific phenotype‐related criteria for variant classification can be affected by the ascertainment of the patient population, and that this should be considered when interpreting results of gene‐testing.
the use of phenotype‐related criteria in the ACMG/AMP variant classification guidelines can be affected by the patient population under investigation.
, in general, the use of gene/syndrome‐specified ACMG‐AMP guidelines is a good approach to improve the utility of these guidelines for clinical interpretation of genetic test results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of phenotype‐related ACMG/AMP criteria in the clinical setting should be informed by the patient population under consideration.
the weight of a phenotype‐based criterion for variant classification can depend on the ascertainment of the patient population.
the weight of patient phenotype in the ACMG/AMP classification framework is not a constant and should be adjusted for differences in patient ascertainment.
